etymologies.etymologyHTML: Borrowed into Middle English from Old French latitude, from Latin lātitūdō (“breadth, width, latitude”), from lātus (“broad, wide”), from older stlātus.

definitions.definition: (geography, astronomy, countable) The angular distance north or south from a planet's equator, measured along the meridian of that particular point.

quote.citation: 1880, Arthur Herbert Church, Food: Some Account of Its Sources, Constituents and Uses‎[1], London: Chapman and Hall, page 72:
quote.text: The oat is hardier than wheat, and ripens in higher latitudes.

quote.citation: 2011, Ralph D. Sawyer, Ancient Chinese Warfare‎[2], Basic Books, →ISBN, →LCCN, →OCLC, →OL, page 137:
quote.text: Far from the center of Shang civilization, Wu-ch'eng is located well south of the Yangtze at approximately the same latitude as Ch'ang-sha in the west and Wen-chou in the east.

definitions.definition: (geography) An imaginary line (in the form of a circumference) around a planet running parallel to the planet's equator.
(figurative) The relative freedom from restrictions; scope to do something.

quote.citation: 1834, L[etitia] E[lizabeth] L[andon], chapter XXIV, in Francesca Carrara. […], volume III, London: Richard Bentley, […], (successor to Henry Colburn), →OCLC, page 208:
quote.text: "Love!" ejaculated the Comtesse; "And so throw away the chances of a life upon a month of honey!—I say a month, which is allowing a latitude tenderness never took...

definitions.definition: (astronomy) The angular distance of a heavenly body from the ecliptic.
(photography) The extent to which a light-sensitive material can be over- or underexposed and still achieve an acceptable result.
Extent or scope; e.g. breadth, width or amplitude.
